intro: Japan’s MEXT scholarship runs on two tracks with different calendars. Which one fits your intake year, what it pays, and how each stage works.
description: MEXT Scholarship 2027: embassy and university tracks, stipends, exams and timeline explained.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: MEXT Scholarship 2027: embassy vs university tracks, stipend rates and the real timeline for each intake.
content:
Japan’s MEXT scholarship — the Japanese government’s flagship — pays a monthly stipend, waives tuition and buys your flight, with no service charges at any stage. What confuses applicants is that it runs on two separate rails with different calendars. Right now, in late 2026, one of those rails is open for the 2027 intake, and the other reopens in April 2027 for the 2028 intake. Choosing the right rail is the first strategic decision; everything else follows from it.

The two tracks

The embassy recommendation track is the classic route: you apply to the Japanese embassy in your country, sit written exams and an interview, and if recommended, MEXT in Tokyo confirms the award. The university recommendation track skips the embassy — a Japanese university nominates you directly after its own review, which usually means you first secure an admission decision or a supervisor’s agreement. Embassy applicants choose placement preferences from a broad list; university-track applicants are already attached to a host.

StageEmbassy track (2028 intake)University track (2027 intake)
Application windowApril-May 2027 at the Japanese embassy in your countryAutumn 2026 - early 2027, set by each university
First screeningMay-July 2027: document review, written tests, interview at the embassyUniversity-run review and interview
Secondary screeningAutumn 2027: MEXT Tokyo reviews recommended candidatesMEXT reviews university-nominated candidates
PlacementJan-Feb 2028: university placement confirmedWithin the application cycle
ArrivalApril or Sep/Oct 2028April or Sep/Oct 2027

What the scholarship pays

Monthly stipends for research students — the master’s/PhD entry category — are ¥143,000-144,000, rising to ¥145,000 for doctoral students, with undergraduates receiving ¥117,000. Tuition at national universities is waived, and MEXT covers airfare to and from Japan. A regional supplement of ¥2,000-3,000 a month applies outside Tokyo. No fees are ever charged at any stage — MEXT itself warns against agents claiming otherwise. Age eligibility sits at under 35 for research students, with academic requirements set by the guidelines each cycle.

[[chart:mext-stipends]]

The written exams, demystified

The embassy track’s exam stage scares applicants more than it should, because MEXT publishes past papers officially — the preparation materials are free and finite. Research-student candidates sit an English paper for everyone, a Japanese paper that is often waivable for those entering English-taught programmes, and subject papers (mathematics, physics, chemistry and so on) depending on the field declared in the application. Scores at the first screening decide who reaches the interview; the interview then weighs the research plan more heavily than the exam sheet. Candidates who spend November and December on two past papers a week routinely outperform those who treat exams as an afterthought.

One structural quirk rewards patience: research students arrive as non-regular students first — a six-month preparatory period in which you take courses, refine the research plan and pass the graduate school’s own entrance process — before matriculating to the degree. The stipend runs the entire time, including the preparation months.

Which track should you choose?

  • Embassy track suits applicants who want maximum programme freedom: you can be placed at nearly any national university after passing screening, and you do not need a professor’s agreement first. The trade-off is the written exams — English, Japanese (for some categories) and subject papers — plus a long pipeline: apply April 2027, land in Japan April 2028.
  • University track suits applicants who already know their supervisor or programme and can start in 2027. Deadlines sit between this winter and early spring, set by each university. It removes the exam gauntlet but narrows your options to the university doing the nominating.
  • Run both if you can. They do not conflict until final placement, and the document piles overlap almost entirely.

The embassy-track file, prepared properly

The application guidelines are strict about forms: the placement preference form, the field-of-study and research plan (the single most-read document), the health certificate filled in by a medical doctor, and recommendation letters on the embassy’s terms. The research plan rewards concreteness — a defined question, a method, a reason it must be done in Japan — over ambition. Written exams for research students focus on English and, depending on category, Japanese and subject papers; past papers are published officially, which makes preparation unusually fair.

Do not send documents to MEXT in Tokyo directly — the ministry rejects them; everything routes through the embassy, and schedules differ by country.
